sections.title: The honest picture for a fresher

blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a fresher. Standards and tools change (OWASP Top 10 editions, TLS versions, certificate exams), so check the official source named in the text before relying on a detail. Practise only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

Cybersecurity is a growing field, but **"entry level" security jobs are scarce compared with the number of people who want them.** Many employers hire into security from development, system administration, networking or IT support. That is good news for you: a Java full stack background is a real advantage, and the job titles below are realistic doors.

| Role | What a fresher does | Skills that matter |
|---|---|---|
| **SOC analyst (L1)** | triage alerts, read logs, escalate, follow playbooks | networking, Windows and Linux logs, SIEM basics, attention, shift work |
| **Junior application security engineer / security-focused developer** | review code and designs, run scanners, help fix findings, secure pipelines | secure coding, OWASP Top 10, a language (Java), Git, CI |
| **Vulnerability management analyst** | run scans, validate and prioritise findings, track fixes | CVSS, scanners, patching process, communication |
| **Junior penetration tester** | assist on web or network tests, write findings | web security, Burp, Linux, reporting. Usually needs proof of lab work |
| **Cloud security associate** | review IAM, configuration and logs in AWS or Azure | cloud basics, IAM, CloudTrail, scripting |
| **GRC analyst** | policies, risk registers, audits, evidence collection | frameworks (ISO 27001, NIST), writing, process |
| **Security intern / trainee** | whatever the team needs | curiosity and reliability |

Where they are: IT services companies, managed security service providers (MSSPs) that run SOCs for many clients, banks and insurers, product companies, consultancies and the "Big 4" advisory firms. Job posts change often, so read several and note which skills repeat.

Working as a Java developer and then moving into AppSec or DevSecOps is one of the most common and best-paid routes. If a security job does not come immediately, a developer job at a company with a security team, where you volunteer for security work, keeps you moving toward your goal.
blocks.title: Developer-first is a strategy, not a detour

blocks.text:
Certificates help get past filters and structure your learning, but **they do not replace skills.** Do not collect them. Confirm current exam names, prices and prerequisites on the issuer's site before you plan.

| Certificate | Level and focus | When it helps |
|---|---|---|
| **CompTIA Security+** | vendor-neutral foundation across threats, architecture, operations, governance | a common baseline requirement in job posts; a good first certificate |
| **ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity (CC)** | entry level concepts | a low-cost start; check current training and exam offers |
| **Google Cybersecurity Certificate** (Coursera) | guided course for beginners | learning path, little recognition on its own |
| **eJPT** (INE) | practical entry-level pentesting exam in a lab | proves hands-on basics |
| **CEH** (EC-Council) | broad ethical hacking theory | frequently listed in Indian job posts, though many practitioners favour practical certificates |
| **CompTIA CySA+ / Blue Team Level 1** | analyst and defender skills | SOC career path |
| **OSCP** (OffSec) | hard, 24-hour practical penetration test | strongly respected, but a later goal rather than a first certificate |
| **AWS Security Specialty, Azure AZ-500** | cloud security | after you have cloud experience |
| **CISSP, CISM, CISA** | management and audit | later in a career; CISSP requires years of experience |

A practical order for you: **fundamentals (this tree) → Security+ (if job posts ask for it) → one practical path (eJPT or Blue Team Level 1) → cloud certificate that matches your AWS skills.**

Tick these honestly. Anything below "can do" is your next study item.

| Area | Can you... |
|---|---|
| **Foundations** | explain CIA, risk, STRIDE, defence in depth, least privilege? |
| **Linux and networking** | use `grep`, `awk`, `ss`, `chmod`; subnet a /26; read a TCP handshake; explain DNS and TLS? |
| **Cryptography** | pick hash vs HMAC vs AES-GCM vs RSA correctly; store passwords properly? |
| **Web security** | exploit and fix SQL injection and XSS in a lab; explain CSRF and IDOR; describe SSRF? |
| **Auth** | explain sessions vs JWT, OAuth with PKCE, MFA and Spring Security configuration? |
| **Secure Java** | validate input, avoid secrets in Git, scan dependencies, write security tests? |
| **Defence** | read a log and spot a brute force; describe the incident response phases? |
| **Cloud and DevSecOps** | write a least-privilege IAM policy; add scanning to a pipeline? |
| **Practice** | have solved labs on a platform and written them up? |
| **Communication** | write a clear finding and explain a risk to a non-technical person? |

Adjust the pace to your time. The aim is to **finish with proof of work.**

| Month | Focus | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | foundations, Linux, networking (parts 1 and 2); OverTheWire Bandit; TryHackMe pre-security | a notes repository; a home lab with two VMs |
| **2** | cryptography and web attacks (parts 3 and 4); Juice Shop and PortSwigger labs | ten written lab summaries |
| **3** | authentication and secure Java (parts 5 and 6) | your "break and fix" Spring Boot project on GitHub with tests |
| **4** | defence, logs and incident response (part 7); Wazuh home SIEM; CyberDefenders | three detections plus an incident write-up |
| **5** | cloud and DevSecOps (part 8); a secure pipeline for your project | a CI workflow with scans and a short README |
| **6** | interviews; apply; optionally sit Security+ | a polished profile, 5 mock interviews, applications sent |

- Put security work under **Projects and Labs**, not under Experience. Learning is real and worth showing, but it is not job experience, and recruiters and interviewers notice when the two are mixed.
- Describe each project with **what you built or tested, the tools, what you found and what you fixed**, plus a link to the repository or write-up. Numbers help ("fixed 5 vulnerabilities; added 12 security tests").
- Show a **short GitHub profile** with a readable README on each project. Remove secrets and anything you were not allowed to publish. Do not publish step-by-step solutions to active challenges or confidential details of any employer.
- On LinkedIn, follow security communities and share short learning notes. Quality beats volume.
- Join communities: local **OWASP** and **null** chapters, college security clubs, CTF teams on CTFtime. They are where referrals happen.

Security interviews for freshers mix **fundamentals, scenarios and a little coding**. Interviewers want to see structured thinking more than memorised lists.

### A structure for scenario questions

> **Clarify → Contain → Investigate → Remediate → Prevent → Communicate**

1. **Clarify:** ask what you know and do not know (what system, when, what data, who is affected).
2. **Contain:** stop the damage first, in the least disruptive way.
3. **Investigate:** logs, timeline, scope, root cause.
4. **Remediate:** remove the cause and restore safely.
5. **Prevent:** the control that would have stopped or detected it.
6. **Communicate:** who must be told, and what you record.

### Questions you should be able to answer in 60 seconds

1. What are the CIA triad and an example of each failing?
2. Difference between authentication and authorisation?
3. Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption: when is each used?
4. Hashing vs encryption vs encoding?
5. What happens when you type `https://` in the browser? (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP)
6. SQL injection: what, why, how to prevent?
7. XSS types and defences?
8. CSRF and how SameSite and tokens help?
9. What is a man-in-the-middle attack and how does TLS stop it?
10. IDS vs IPS; stateful firewall vs WAF?
11. Black, grey and white box testing?
12. What is the OWASP Top 10, and which category is number one?
13. How should passwords be stored?
14. Explain session vs JWT authentication.
15. What is least privilege? Give a cloud example.
16. What does a SOC analyst do on a failed-login alert?
17. How do you secure a REST API?
18. What is a zero-day? A CVE? CVSS?
19. How would you respond to a suspected phishing click?
20. How do you stay current? (name two sources you actually follow)

"Authenticate every request with short-lived tokens over HTTPS only. Authorise on the server for each object and function, deny by default. Validate and size-limit input with DTOs, and use parameterised queries. Rate-limit, return generic errors, log security events without secrets, set security headers and strict CORS, keep dependencies patched, and test the unhappy paths. Keep secrets in a secret manager and give the service a least-privilege database account."
blocks.title: "How would you secure a REST API?"

blocks.text: "Stop at the minimum needed to confirm, do not access or change data, and report it through the site's security contact or disclosure programme with clear steps. I would not publish it or ask for payment."
blocks.title: "What would you do if you accidentally found a vulnerability in a website you do not own?"

blocks.text: Use a short story: the problem, what you built, the vulnerabilities you found or fixed (name them), the tools, one thing you got wrong and learned, and what you would improve. A concrete example of an IDOR you fixed with an ownership check and a test beats a list of tools.
blocks.title: "Tell me about a security project you built."

blocks.text:
### Keeping up to date

Sources worth following: the **OWASP Cheat Sheet Series** (practical and concise), **PortSwigger** research and labs, **CISA** and **CERT-In** advisories, the **NVD** (National Vulnerability Database), **SANS** reading room and newsletters, and security news sites. Choose a few and read regularly, rather than skimming everything.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Entry-level security roles exist but are competitive, and a developer background is an advantage
- Certificates help but projects and labs prove skill
- List learning under Projects and Labs and never as work experience
- Use clarify, contain, investigate, remediate, prevent and communicate for scenario answers
- Prepare 60-second answers to the core fundamentals
- Build a break-and-fix project, a home SIEM and a secure pipeline as proof

51 original questions on 11 areas. *Recall* questions test a definition or a rule. *Scenario* questions give you a situation, a log or a snippet and ask what is wrong or what to do. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which role is the most natural first step for a Java developer interested in security?
o: application security engineer or a security-focused developer role
items.w: AppSec uses existing skills in code, HTTP, databases and frameworks. A developer role with security duties is also a recognised route.

items.q: *(Recall)* A Tier 1 SOC analyst most needs
o: log reading, networking basics, SIEM familiarity and careful triage
items.w: L1 analysts judge alerts quickly and escalate correctly.

items.q: *(Recall)* GRC stands for
items.w: GRC analysts work on policies, risk registers, audits and frameworks such as ISO 27001.

items.q: *(Recall)* An MSSP is
o: a managed security service provider that runs security operations for many client companies
items.w: Many entry-level SOC jobs are at MSSPs, because they run 24x7 monitoring for multiple clients.

items.q: *(Recall)* CompTIA Security+ is best described as
o: an advanced management certificate for senior leaders
a vendor-neutral foundation certificate frequently listed in entry-level job posts
items.w: It covers broad fundamentals. It does not prove hands-on depth by itself.

items.q: *(Recall)* eJPT is known as
o: a practical entry-level penetration testing exam done in a lab
items.w: Practical exams show that you can do tasks, not only recall terms.

items.q: *(Recall)* OSCP is generally regarded as
o: a demanding hands-on penetration testing exam, usually a later goal
items.w: It tests the ability to compromise machines in a timed lab, which is hard for beginners.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A fresher has no projects and plans to sit five certificates in six months. A better plan is
o: build lab and project proof (write-ups, a break-and-fix app, a home SIEM) and sit one or two relevant certificates
items.w: Certificates open doors, but projects show that you can do the work and give you things to discuss in interviews.

items.q: *(Recall)* On a CV, personal lab work and projects should be listed under
o: Work Experience, as a security analyst
items.w: Learning is valuable but is not job experience, and interviewers will probe it.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A candidate lists "penetration tested production banking systems" for a weekend lab. In an interview this will
o: collapse under follow-up questions and damage trust, so describe the real lab and what was learned instead
items.w: Be accurate. Honest descriptions of real projects stand up to questions.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Your GitHub write-up of an active CTF includes the full solution and flag. The platform's rules forbid that. You should
o: remove it and write about the concept instead
items.w: Respect platform rules. Concept-level write-ups are allowed and more valuable.

items.q: *(Recall)* A good first move in a scenario question such as "a server is infected" is to
o: clarify what is known and then contain the damage
items.w: Clarify first, contain next, then investigate, remediate, prevent and communicate.

items.q: *(Recall)* Encrypting a backup protects which CIA property?
items.w: Without the key, the contents cannot be read.

items.q: *(Scenario)* An asset worth 12,00,000 would lose 50% in one incident, which happens once every 3 years. The ALE is
*(Recall)* STRIDE is used for
items.w: Spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A /27 subnet has how many usable host addresses?
items.w: 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus network and broadcast.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which is the correct TCP connection setup?
items.w: The client starts, the server answers, the client confirms.

items.q: *(Recall)* Port 443 is used by
items.w: HTTP over TLS. Port 80 is HTTP, 22 SSH and 25 SMTP.

items.q: *(Scenario)* "What happens when you type https://example.com in a browser?" Which sequence is the most complete?
o: DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS handshake with certificate validation, HTTP request and response over the encrypted channel
items.w: Each step has security implications: DNS spoofing, port scans, certificate checks and HTTP-level attacks.

items.q: *(Recall)* The difference between hashing and encryption is that
o: encryption can be reversed with a key, whereas a hash is one-way
items.w: Use hashing for integrity and password storage, encryption for confidentiality.

items.q: *(Recall)* A SHA-256 hash in hexadecimal is how many characters long?
items.w: 256 bits / 4 = 64 hex characters.

items.q: *(Recall)* Symmetric encryption is typically used for
o: encrypting bulk data quickly with a shared key
items.w: Asymmetric cryptography exchanges keys or signs, then symmetric cryptography carries the data.

items.q: *(Scenario)* An interviewer asks how to prevent SQL injection. The strongest answer is
o: "parameterised queries everywhere, allow-lists for identifiers, a least-privilege database account, generic errors"
items.w: Fix the cause (data mixed into code) and add layers.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Which pair of defences best handles XSS and CSRF respectively?
o: output encoding with a CSP, and SameSite cookies with anti-CSRF tokens
items.w: XSS is about untrusted data becoming script. CSRF is about unwanted authenticated requests.

items.q: *(Scenario)* "How do you store passwords?" The best short answer is
o: salted, slow hashing with Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2, plus MFA
items.w: The hash must be expensive to guess and unique per user.

items.q: *(Scenario)* When would you prefer server-side sessions to JWTs in a browser app?
o: when you need easy revocation and the app is a classic web app, using a protected cookie
items.w: Server sessions are simple to invalidate. JWTs shine for stateless service-to-service use but are hard to revoke before expiry.

items.q: *(Recall)* Least privilege means
o: each identity gets only the access it needs for its task
items.w: It limits damage when an identity is compromised.

items.q: *(Scenario)* In a cloud role review you see Action "*" on Resource "*". You would
o: flag it and propose a policy restricted to the exact actions and resources the workload uses
items.w: Full wildcards are the standard anti-pattern. Use Access Analyzer and CloudTrail to find what is really used.

items.q: *(Recall)* A zero-day is
o: a vulnerability unknown to the vendor, with no patch available
items.w: Defenders use compensating controls until a patch exists.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A CVSS v3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H has a base score of
items.w: Network, low complexity, no privileges or user interaction, high impact on all three: 9.8, Critical.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A 12-character random password drawn from 94 printable characters has about how many bits of entropy?
*(Scenario)* An employee reports that they entered their password on a fake login page from an e-mail. The best first response is
o: reset their password, revoke sessions, check sign-in logs and mailbox rules, and search for the same e-mail in other inboxes
items.w: Assume the credentials are compromised. Contain, then check what the attacker did and who else received it.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A server shows thousands of failed SSH logins followed by one success from the same IP, and a new user was created minutes later. What do you conclude and do?
o: likely compromise: isolate the host, preserve evidence, disable the new account, investigate persistence, rotate credentials, rebuild
items.w: A successful login after many failures, followed by account creation, fits brute force plus persistence.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A developer finds an access key in a commit made three months ago in a private repository. The correct response is
o: rotate the key now, review CloudTrail for use, and add secret scanning to prevent a repeat
items.w: History retains the key, and many people may have cloned the repository. Rotation is the control.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Customers report that a shopping site charged them different prices than shown. Investigation shows the price is sent in a hidden form field. The fix is
o: use the price from the server-side catalogue and ignore any price in the request
items.w: Never trust client-side values for decisions the server owns.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A security scan shows the app's TLS configuration allows TLS 1.0 and weak ciphers. The recommended fix is
o: disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and weak ciphers, support TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and enable HSTS
items.w: Old protocol versions have known weaknesses. Modern clients support 1.2 and 1.3.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A team wants to log request bodies to debug problems. What risk should you raise?
o: logs may then contain passwords, tokens and personal data, so mask sensitive fields or avoid logging bodies
items.w: Logs are widely accessible and long lived. Treat them as sensitive.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A new endpoint lets users download their invoice as PDF using /invoice/{id}/pdf. What test do you run first?
o: log in as two users and request user A's invoice with user B's session
items.w: Object-level authorisation is the likely weakness. This test costs a minute.

items.q: *(Recall)* After an incident, the "lessons learned" meeting should be
o: blameless, producing concrete improvements to controls and processes
items.w: Blame leads to concealment. Improvement leads to fewer incidents.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which statement is true about security scanners?
o: they produce false positives and miss logic flaws, so results need human triage
items.w: Use them as one input among several.

items.q: *(Recall)* The OWASP Cheat Sheet Series is
o: a set of concise, practical security guidance documents
items.w: Examples: Password Storage, SQL Injection Prevention, Session Management.

items.q: *(Recall)* CERT-In is
o: India's national agency for cybersecurity incident response and advisories
items.w: It issues advisories and sets incident reporting directions for organisations in India.

items.q: *(Recall)* The NVD is
o: the US National Vulnerability Database, which lists CVEs with scores and references
items.w: It is a standard reference for vulnerability details and CVSS scores.

items.q: *(Recall)* You are asked by a friend to "check if their ex's account password is weak". You should
o: refuse, because accessing someone's account without authorisation is illegal and unethical
items.w: Authorisation is the line between security work and a crime.

items.q: *(Scenario)* During an authorised test you accidentally access a file with real customer records. You should
o: stop, avoid reading further, note what happened and inform your engagement contact immediately
items.w: Handle sensitive data minimally and report promptly, as agreed in the rules of engagement.

items.q: *(Recall)* Why is non-disclosure and careful handling of client data central to a security career?
o: clients trust testers with their most sensitive weaknesses and data; breaches of that trust end careers
items.w: Reputation is the main asset in this field.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A fresher has three months and wants a security portfolio. Which plan gives the best proof?
o: complete 10 labs with write-ups, build a break-and-fix Spring Boot project with tests, and set up a small home SIEM with three detections
items.w: Concrete artefacts that you can show and explain beat passive consumption.

items.q: *(Scenario)* You have limited time. Which order of study fits an AppSec-focused fresher?
o: foundations and networking, cryptography, web attacks, authentication and secure Java, then defence and cloud
items.w: It follows the tree: the basics support everything else, and secure coding is your biggest advantage.

items.q: *(Recall)* Why should you practise explaining a vulnerability to a non-technical person?
o: security work requires convincing managers and developers to act on findings
because jargon is a legal requirement
items.w: Communication decides whether findings get fixed.

items.q: *(Recall)* The main difference between an IDS and an IPS is that an IPS
o: sits inline and can block the traffic it detects, while an IDS only alerts
items.w: An IPS can stop attacks in real time but a false positive can block legitimate users.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A candidate is asked "How would you secure a REST API?" and answers "use HTTPS". The better answer adds
o: authentication and per-object authorisation, input validation, rate limiting, generic errors, logging without secrets, security headers and patched dependencies
items.w: HTTPS protects transport only. The rest of the checklist covers the attacks that happen inside the encrypted channel.

items.question: Why might a developer job first be a good route into AppSec?
items.answer: Application security relies on reading and writing code, understanding frameworks and working with developers. Experience as a developer, plus security work and projects, makes the move credible.

items.question: Name two practical, entry-level steps that prove skill better than a certificate alone.
items.answer: Written lab or CTF reports and a break-and-fix project on GitHub (or a home SIEM with custom detections).

items.question: Where should a fresher list lab work on a CV?
items.answer: Under Projects and Labs, described accurately. It should not appear as work experience.

items.question: Give the six-step structure for answering a security scenario question.
items.answer: Clarify, contain, investigate, remediate, prevent, communicate.

items.question: What is the first thing you do with a suspected phishing click?
items.answer: Treat the account as compromised: reset credentials, revoke sessions, check mailbox rules and sign-in logs, and look for other recipients.

items.question: Name three sources to keep up with security news and techniques.
items.answer: For example the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, PortSwigger research, and CISA or CERT-In advisories.
